section.title: True Fasting and the Sabbath
section.sectionRationale: This oracle exposes the gap between religious performance and covenant obedience with surgical precision. Israel fasts, bows the head, spreads sackcloth, and asks God why He does not notice; God answers that the fast He has chosen looks like loosing chains, feeding the hungry, and welcoming the homeless. It is one of Scripture's clearest statements that worship without justice is empty.
section.thesis: The fasting God desires is not ritual self-denial but active justice, breaking every yoke, feeding the hungry, sheltering the homeless, and honoring the Sabbath as a delight, and only this kind of worship brings the light, healing, and guidance God promises.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the LORD's charge against empty ritual; the fast God has actually chosen; and the promised blessing of light, healing, and satisfaction for those who honor the Sabbath and pursue justice.

units.label: Why have we fasted, and You have not seen?

verses.text: “Cry aloud, do not hold back! Raise your voice like a ram’s horn. Declare to My people their transgression and to the house of Jacob their sins.

For day after day they seek Me and delight to know My ways, like a nation that does what is right and does not forsake the justice of their God. They ask Me for righteous judgments; they delight in the nearness of God.”
“Why have we fasted, and You have not seen? Why have we humbled ourselves, and You have not noticed?” “Behold, on the day of your fast, you do as you please, and you oppress all your workers.
You fast with contention and strife to strike viciously with your fist. You cannot fast as you do today and have your voice be heard on high.
Is this the fast I have chosen: a day for a man to deny himself, to bow his head like a reed, and to spread out sackcloth and ashes? Will you call this a fast and a day acceptable to the LORD?

units.label: The fast that I have chosen
units.note: break the chains, feed the hungry, clothe the naked

verses.text: Isn’t this the fast that I have chosen: to break the chains of wickedness, to untie the cords of the {{ol|yoke}}, to set the oppressed free and tear off every yoke?
Isn’t it to share your bread with the hungry, to bring the poor and homeless into your home, to clothe the naked when you see him, and not to turn away from your own flesh and blood?
Then your light will break forth like the dawn, and your healing will come quickly. Your righteousness will go before you, and the glory of the LORD will be your rear guard.
Then you will call, and the LORD will answer; you will cry out, and He will say, ‘Here I am.’ If you remove the yoke from your midst, the pointing of the finger and malicious talk,
and if you give yourself to the hungry and satisfy the afflicted soul, then your light will go forth in the darkness, and your night will be like noonday.
The LORD will always guide you; He will satisfy you in a sun-scorched land and strengthen your frame. You will be like a well-watered garden, like a spring whose waters never fail.
Your people will rebuild the ancient ruins; you will restore the age-old foundations; you will be called {{gader|Repairer of the Breach}}, Restorer of the Streets of Dwelling.

If you turn your foot from breaking the Sabbath, from doing as you please on My holy day, if you call the Sabbath a delight, and the LORD’s holy day honorable, if you honor it by not going your own way or seeking your own pleasure or speaking idle words,
then you will delight yourself in the LORD, and I will make you ride on the heights of the land and feed you with the heritage of your father Jacob.” For the mouth of the LORD has spoken.

ol.gloss: Yoke, the wooden bar laid across the neck of a laboring animal or an oppressed person. The fast God chooses tears off every ol, whether the yoke of slavery, injustice, or oppressive speech, verse 9's pointing of the finger; Jesus offers a different yoke entirely, easy and light, Matthew 11:29-30, the rest this yoke-breaking fast anticipates.

gader.gloss: Repairer of the breach, one who rebuilds a broken wall. The title given to those who practice true justice and honor the Sabbath pictures restoration of what sin and neglect have ruined, both the literal ruins of Jerusalem and, by extension, broken relationships and communities repaired through righteous living.

basic.context: The people fast and wonder why God seems not to notice. God answers plainly: their fasting is paired with oppression, exploiting workers and quarreling, so it cannot rise to Him. The fast He actually wants looks like loosing chains, feeding the hungry, and sheltering the homeless, joined with honoring the Sabbath as delight rather than burden.
basic.hermeneutics: This is not a rejection of fasting or the Sabbath as such, but of religious ritual detached from justice and mercy. Isaiah insists that true worship and social righteousness are inseparable; you cannot fast acceptably while oppressing your workers, and you cannot claim to seek God while ignoring the hungry at your door.
basic.originalLanguages: The fast God chooses breaks every ol, yoke, whether of wickedness, oppression, or cruel speech. And those who practice this justice, alongside honoring the Sabbath, earn the title gader poretz, repairer of the breach, rebuilders of what was ruined.
basic.typology: The true fast that frees the oppressed and feeds the hungry anticipates Jesus' own mission statement, to proclaim good news to the poor, to set at liberty those who are oppressed, Luke 4:18, itself drawn from Isaiah 61. The yoke torn off here anticipates the easy yoke Christ offers in its place.
basic.christ: Jesus reads His mission directly out of Isaiah's language of freedom for the oppressed, and in Matthew 25 He identifies Himself with the hungry fed, the naked clothed, and the stranger welcomed, as if done to Him directly, the very acts this chapter names as true fasting.
basic.god: God is not impressed by self-denial disconnected from mercy; He measures worship by whether it produces justice for the vulnerable. Yet He is also generous beyond the demand, promising light, healing, guidance, and satisfaction to those who actually live this way.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 25:35-40 has Jesus identify with the hungry, naked, and stranger cared for. Matthew 11:28-30 offers an easy yoke in place of heavy burdens. James 1:27 defines pure religion as caring for orphans and widows in distress.
basic.oneStory: God has always cared more about hearts turned to justice and mercy than about ritual performed for its own sake. This chapter's true fast, breaking yokes and feeding the hungry, finds its fullest embodiment in Jesus, who both proclaims freedom to the oppressed and identifies Himself with the hungry and homeless He calls His people to serve.

context.literary:
Isaiah 58 is built as a trial in which the accused is a pious people. It opens with a command to the prophet to shout like a ram's horn, verse 1, and the first charge is a surprise, because verse 2 describes the people as seeking God 'day after day' and delighting in His ways. The speech then gives their complaint in their own voice, 'Why have we fasted, and You have not seen?' verse 3, and God's reply cuts it off at once, 'on the day of your fast, you do as you please, and you oppress all your workers.' The question form of verses 5 and 6, 'Is this the fast I have chosen? ... Isn't this the fast that I have chosen?' is a classic prophetic device that makes the hearers supply the answer themselves.

The central section, verses 6 to 12, is held together by a series of 'if' and 'then' clauses. 'If you remove the yoke from your midst' in verse 9 and 'if you give yourself to the hungry' in verse 10 are paired with promises that begin 'Then your light will break forth,' verse 8, 'Then you will call,' verse 9, and 'your light will go forth in the darkness,' verse 10. The word yoke frames the whole unit, since verse 6 speaks of tearing off every yoke and verse 9 of removing the yoke from the people's midst.

The last two verses turn from the fast to the Sabbath with the same conditional form, 'If you turn your foot ... then you will delight yourself in the LORD,' verses 13 and 14. One Hebrew word, chephets, links the beginning, the middle and the end. The people 'delight' in God's ways in verse 2, find their own 'pleasure' on the day of fasting in verse 3, and are told not to seek 'your own pleasure' on the Sabbath in verse 13. The chapter sits between the lament of a people who feel unheard and the declaration in Isaiah 59:2 that their sins have built barriers, and it leads into the great light of Isaiah 60.
context.historical:
Fasting was a normal part of Israel's religious life. People fasted at times of national crisis, in sackcloth and ashes, as the Ninevites did and as Joel calls the people to do, Jonah 3:5-8 and Joel 2:12-13. The law's one required fast, on the Day of Atonement, was described by the verb 'humble yourselves,' Leviticus 16:29-31. After the destruction of Jerusalem the people also kept fasts in the fifth and seventh months for seventy years, and when they asked the priests whether to continue, Zechariah was told to ask them, 'was it really for Me that you fasted?' Zechariah 7:5. The charge in Isaiah 58 is the same one, and the sequel there is the same, 'Administer true justice. Show loving devotion and compassion ... Do not oppress the widow or the fatherless, the foreigner or the poor,' Zechariah 7:9-10.

The oppression of workers is not an abstraction. The law told employers to pay a poor hired hand each day before sunset, Deuteronomy 24:14-15, and Jeremiah condemned a king who made his countrymen 'serve without pay,' Jeremiah 22:13. When the king and people of Jerusalem freed their Hebrew slaves and then took them back, Jeremiah told them they had not proclaimed freedom, Jeremiah 34:8-17. In the generation after the exile, Nehemiah found nobles exacting interest from their own countrymen and enslaving their children, Nehemiah 5:1-13. These are the yokes and chains of verse 6.

The Sabbath was joined to the same concern from the start. The commandment in Deuteronomy 5:14-15 gives rest to servants and the foreigner, and grounds it in the memory that Israel was a slave in Egypt. The yoke of verses 6 and 9 is the bar of a yoke, the kind of word God uses in Leviticus 26:13, 'I broke the bars of your yoke.' The people were being asked to do for others what God had done for them.
context.canonical:
The charge that devotion without justice is empty runs through the prophets. Isaiah's first chapter says God will not listen to prayers offered with hands full of blood, Isaiah 1:11-17. Amos hears God hate the feasts and prefer that justice roll on like a river, Amos 5:21-24. Hosea reports God's desire for mercy and not sacrifice, Hosea 6:6, and Micah says what the LORD requires is to act justly, love mercy and walk humbly, Micah 6:6-8. Isaiah 58 is the most developed of these, because it is about a specific practice, fasting, and answers the very complaint that God has not noticed.

The chapter also lies behind the way Jesus describes His own work. At Nazareth He reads from Isaiah 61 in the synagogue, and Luke's version includes the words 'to release the oppressed,' Luke 4:18, a phrase that matches Isaiah 58:6 in the Greek Septuagint and is not in the Hebrew of Isaiah 61:1. The two chapters of Isaiah are fused in Jesus' announcement. He teaches His disciples how to fast, Matthew 6:16-18, answers the question why they do not, Matthew 9:14-15, and identifies Himself with the hungry, the stranger, the naked and the prisoner, Matthew 25:35-40.

The early church picked up the practical side. James defines pure religion as caring for orphans and widows in their distress, James 1:27, and warns that faith with no deeds is dead, James 2:14-17. John asks how the love of God can abide in someone who sees a brother in need and withholds compassion, 1 John 3:17-18. Acts shows the first believers sharing with anyone in need, Acts 2:44-45 and 4:34-35.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The prophet is not addressing the openly wicked. He is addressing people who consider themselves among the most religious, who pray, ask for righteous decisions and fast with some hardship, and who are confused that God does not seem to respond. His purpose is to show them that the silence is not on God's side. He wants them to stop treating the fast as a technique for getting a hearing and to see what it was always meant to express.

The positive teaching is that a day of self-denial should lead to a life of giving. The list in verses 6 and 7 is concrete: break chains, release the oppressed, share bread, shelter the homeless, clothe the naked and do not turn away from your own family. It is a program for the people who have power over workers, over debt, and over the means of providing a meal. He wanted them to see that the fast God wants would cost them something more than a meal.

He also meant this to be good news. The long list of promises in verses 8 to 12, light, healing, an answered prayer, guidance, strength, a watered garden and a rebuilt city, is God's invitation to a people who believed they had been left alone. The Sabbath coda, verses 13 and 14, is meant to restore a day that had become a burden and a business into a delight in the LORD.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage does not abolish fasting. The question 'Is this the fast I have chosen?' assumes that there is a fast God has chosen, and Jesus later says to His disciples, 'When you fast,' Matthew 6:16, and expects that they will after He is taken away, Matthew 9:15. What is rejected is fasting as a performance, which Jesus also warns against, Matthew 6:16-18. The passage prescribes the combination, a heart that is humble before God and hands that are open to people. Jesus makes the same point about tithing when He tells the Pharisees to practice justice, mercy and faithfulness 'without neglecting the former,' Matthew 23:23.

Care is needed with the promises. The 'if' and 'then' clauses are covenant promises to a community, and they are not a formula by which generosity buys health or wealth. 'Your healing will come quickly,' verse 8, is the language of national restoration, a wound closing, and it should not be read as a guarantee that giving will cure illness. The prophet also does not prescribe a particular economic or political arrangement. He names deeds, such as paying workers, feeding the hungry and ending exploitation, and leaves the means to the situation.

The Sabbath verses are also covenant instructions, and Christians have understood them differently. Some keep a weekly day of rest and worship, and others see in Christ the fulfillment of the Sabbath, Hebrews 4:9-10, and hold that no one should judge another on the matter, Romans 14:5 and Colossians 2:16-17. What carries over for all is the spirit of verse 13, that God's holy time is for delighting in Him, not for pursuing our own business.

debates.question: Is the people's devotion in verse 2 sincere or ironic?

views.label: Sincere but misdirected
views.case: The language of seeking God daily, delighting to know His ways and asking for righteous judgments is meant straightforwardly. These are devout people, and that is why God's rebuke is so sharp, since their zeal has not touched their conduct. Jeremiah 22:16 says that to know God is to take up the cause of the poor and needy, so the knowledge they delighted in was missing its essence.

views.label: Ironic
views.case: God says they delight in His ways 'like a nation that does what is right,' and the 'like' suggests an appearance. On this reading the verse is sarcastic, reporting how the people see themselves while the next verses expose the reality, as with Isaiah 1:11-15, where God refuses prayers from bloody hands.

views.label: Mixed community
views.case: Some of the people were genuine seekers and others were going through the motions. The prophet addresses the community as a whole, and the warning applies to whoever recognizes themselves.

debates.bearing: On any reading the point is the same. Outward devotion is not evidence of obedience, and the people most at risk are those who are sure they are doing everything right.

debates.question: Does the chapter set ritual against justice, or hold them together?

views.label: It dismisses ritual in favor of justice
views.case: The fast 'I have chosen' is described entirely in terms of deeds, and the ritual of verse 5, bowing the head like a reed and spreading sackcloth, is not endorsed. Some read this as a prophetic preference for ethics over cult, in line with Hosea 6:6, 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice.'

views.label: It requires both
views.case: The chapter ends by commanding Sabbath observance and promising delight in the LORD, verses 13 and 14, so ritual is not abolished. Jesus' words on tithing, 'practice justice, mercy, and faithfulness, without neglecting the former,' Matthew 23:23, fit this reading, as does His assumption that His followers will fast.

views.label: It redefines what the ritual is for
views.case: Fasting was meant to express humility and dependence on God, and verses 6 and 7 say that true humility shows itself in treating others rightly. The ritual is not canceled but given its proper content.

debates.bearing: The second and third readings fit the whole chapter, which begins with fasting, ends with the Sabbath and joins them with justice. Worship and justice are not rivals, but worship without justice is worthless.

study.originalLanguages:
One word runs through the chapter and exposes its irony. In verse 2 the people 'delight' to know God's ways and 'delight' in His nearness, and the Hebrew verb is chaphets, to take pleasure or to desire. In verse 3, on the day of their fast, they 'do as you please,' and the noun is chephets, which can mean pleasure and also business or affairs. In verse 13 the Sabbath is not for 'doing as you please' or 'seeking your own pleasure.' It is the word God uses of Himself, as in 'what I please,' Isaiah 55:11, and 'the good pleasure of the LORD,' Isaiah 53:10. The point of the chapter is whose pleasure governs a holy day, ours or His.

The people's self-description in verse 3, 'we have humbled ourselves,' uses the Hebrew idiom of afflicting the soul, the phrase the law uses for the Day of Atonement, 'you shall humble yourselves,' Leviticus 16:29. The same root recurs in verse 10, where they are told to 'satisfy the afflicted soul.' It is a bitter turn. The people who afflict their own souls for a day are called to relieve the soul of someone who is afflicted every day. The language of self-denial is the language of verse 5, 'a day for a man to deny himself.' The prophet asks them to turn their attention from their own hunger to someone else's.

The yoke of verses 6 and 9 is described in the vocabulary of the wooden bar and the straps that hold it, motah, the 'cords' of which are to be untied and the whole of which is to be torn off. The related plural is the word for the crossbars that God says He broke at the exodus, 'I broke the bars of your yoke,' Leviticus 26:13. What Israel received from God in Egypt they were being asked to give in Judah.

In verse 8 'the glory of the LORD will be your rear guard.' The Hebrew verb behind 'rear guard' is asaph, to gather, and the word means the one who gathers up the stragglers at the back. It is the same word used in Isaiah 52:12, 'the God of Israel is your rear guard,' at the beginning of the new exodus. In Exodus 14:19-20 the angel and the cloud moved behind the camp to protect it. The promise in this chapter is that the divine presence that shielded the people at the Red Sea will guard them again.

Verse 9 closes with the words 'Here I am,' hinneni. It is the answer that people give when God calls them, as Abraham does in Genesis 22:1 and Isaiah in Isaiah 6:8. Here God says it to them. The one who is accused of not noticing says that He is present and ready. The same words begin Isaiah 65:1, where God says them to a nation that did not call His name. Finally the Sabbath in verse 13 is called an oneg, a delight, a warm word, and 'the LORD's holy day' is to be honored, a word built on the root kavod, built on the root for glory and weight.

typology.type: Breaking the yoke and setting the oppressed free, verse 6
typology.fulfillment: The yoke bars that God broke in Egypt, Leviticus 26:13, and the liberty proclaimed in the Jubilee, Leviticus 25:10, are the background of the prophet's command. Jesus takes it up at Nazareth, where His reading includes 'to release the oppressed,' Luke 4:18, and in the synagogue when He frees a woman bound for eighteen years and asks whether she should not be 'released from her bondage on the Sabbath day,' Luke 13:16. Paul says, 'It is for freedom that Christ has set us free,' Galatians 5:1, and Jesus says, 'if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed,' John 8:36. The type falls short because Isaiah's yokes are social, while Christ also breaks the yoke of sin.

typology.type: Feeding the hungry and welcoming the homeless, verse 7
typology.fulfillment: Jesus identifies Himself with those named in verse 7. At the judgment the King says, 'I was hungry and you gave Me something to eat ... I was a stranger and you took Me in ... I was naked and you clothed Me,' and 'whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers of Mine, you did for Me,' Matthew 25:35-40. Paul says that though He was rich, Christ became poor so that we might become rich, 2 Corinthians 8:9. The correspondence rises from a duty to a person: what is done for the needy is done to Christ. The type falls short because Isaiah's acts of mercy are not the way to salvation, since faith in Christ is.

typology.type: Light breaking forth like the dawn, verses 8 and 10
typology.fulfillment: The promised light finds its fulfillment in Jesus, who says, 'I am the light of the world. Whoever follows Me will never walk in the darkness,' John 8:12. He also tells His disciples, 'You are the light of the world,' and tells them to let their light shine so people 'may see your good deeds and glorify your Father in heaven,' Matthew 5:14-16, which is the same pairing of light and good works as Isaiah 58:10. A little later Isaiah carries the thought on, 'Arise, shine, for your light has come,' Isaiah 60:1. The type falls short because Isaiah's light is promised on condition of the people's actions, whereas Christ is the light first and His people reflect it.

typology.type: Repairer of the Breach, rebuilding the ruins, verse 12
typology.fulfillment: Nehemiah had said, 'Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem,' Nehemiah 2:17, and Isaiah promised a people who would rebuild ancient ruins. In the New Testament James cites Amos's promise that God will 'rebuild the fallen tent of David,' Acts 15:16, applying it to the inclusion of the Gentiles. Jesus speaks of raising up the temple of His body, John 2:19-21, and Paul says believers are being built together into a dwelling place for God, Ephesians 2:22. The type falls short because Isaiah's rebuilding concerns walls and streets, and the new work builds a people.

typology.type: The Sabbath as a delight and the rest it points toward, verses 13 and 14
typology.fulfillment: Jesus declares that 'The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath,' and that the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath, Mark 2:27-28. He invites the weary and burdened to come to Him for rest, and says His yoke is easy and His burden light, Matthew 11:28-30. Hebrews says that 'a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God,' and that the one who enters God's rest rests from his own work, Hebrews 4:9-10. The type falls short because the weekly day is a sign and a taste of a rest that Christ gives in full and that will be complete in the new creation.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ through His reading of Scripture in the synagogue at Nazareth. When He stood up on the Sabbath and read from Isaiah, the passage He chose combined Isaiah 61 with the line from Isaiah 58:6, 'to release the oppressed,' Luke 4:16-19. He then said, 'Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing,' Luke 4:21. The freedom that Isaiah called His people to give to others is the freedom He came to bring. The yoke they were to break He breaks, first of all by His works and finally by the cross.

It leads to Christ in the way He handles the Sabbath. In the synagogue He sees a woman who has been bent over for eighteen years, and He says that this daughter of Abraham, whom Satan has kept bound, should be released from her bondage on the Sabbath day, Luke 13:10-16. Isaiah 58 had said the Sabbath is a delight, joined with loosing chains, and Jesus demonstrates it. He also says that the Sabbath was made for man and that He is Lord of it, Mark 2:27-28. His Sabbath actions are not a break with Isaiah but its enactment.

It leads to Christ in His identification with those named in verse 7. In the parable of the judgment He says that when the hungry were fed, the stranger welcomed and the naked clothed, it was done to Him, Matthew 25:35-40. Paul says that though He was rich He became poor, 2 Corinthians 8:9, so the Lord who calls us to share our bread has Himself given everything.

It leads to Christ as the true self-denial. Verse 5 asks whether the fast is 'a day for a man to deny himself.' Jesus says that anyone who wants to follow Him 'must deny himself and take up his cross,' Mark 8:34, and Philippians tells how He emptied Himself and became obedient to death, Philippians 2:7-8. He also fasted forty days in the wilderness and was hungry, Luke 4:2, so He does not abolish the practice. What He did with His self-denial was to turn it into the life that was given for others. Where the people's fasting produced oppression, His produced a rescue.

He also answers the question of why bridegroom's guests should fast, Matthew 9:14-15. While He is present, it is a time of celebration, and the days of fasting come when He is taken away. The fast of the church is therefore a fast of longing and obedience, never a bargain.

A caution keeps this honest. The chapter does not say that acts of mercy earn salvation, and the New Testament does not read it that way. James says faith without deeds is dead, James 2:17, and Paul says we are saved by grace and not by works, Ephesians 2:8-9. The deeds are the evidence and fruit of a faith in the One who frees us. What Isaiah supplies is the shape of the life that Christ makes possible, and the shape of His own.
study.god:
The God of this chapter is one whose attention cannot be bought. The people ask why He has not seen them fast, and He replies that He has seen everything, the pleasure they pursued and the workers they oppressed, verse 3. This is a God who notices what happens in the workplace and the household and not only what is done in the sanctuary. He cannot be impressed by self-denial that costs the powerful nothing, for 'you cannot fast as you do today and have your voice be heard on high,' verse 4. It matches Isaiah 1:15, where He hides His eyes from hands covered with blood, and Proverbs 21:13, which says the one who shuts his ears to the poor will cry out and not be answered.

He is a God who identifies with the poor. The needy are not a separate category from God. Proverbs says that whoever oppresses the poor 'taunts their Maker,' and that kindness to the poor is 'a loan to the LORD,' Proverbs 14:31 and 19:17. Jeremiah says that to take up the cause of the poor and needy is what it means to know God, Jeremiah 22:16. That is why He can say that a failure to feed the hungry is a failure in worship.

He is also generous beyond what He asks. The promises of verses 8 to 12 are an extraordinary list. Light, healing, righteousness going before, glory at the rear, answered prayer, guidance, strength in the desert, a garden that never fails, and a city rebuilt. He says 'Here I am' to the one who calls, verse 9, a response of immediate presence. The God who is accused of not noticing is the One who has been waiting to answer. The garden image also recalls the restoration of Eden, Isaiah 51:3 and Jeremiah 31:12.

He is a God of holy time. The Sabbath is 'My holy day,' and He desires that it be called a delight, verse 13. The day is not a regulation to be got through but a gift that frees people from the pressure of their own affairs. In Deuteronomy the Sabbath is tied to the memory that He brought Israel out of slavery, Deuteronomy 5:15, and so it belongs with the freeing of the oppressed. The God who gave rest to slaves means His people to give rest to those under them.

He is the God who keeps His word, as the chapter ends, 'For the mouth of the LORD has spoken,' verse 14.

For worship, the chapter says that God is not looking for the loudest or the longest or the hungriest, but for people who are like Him. The question we are invited to ask on any day of devotion is who has been set free because we came before God.

crossReferences.note: Isaiah's first chapter says God is tired of sacrifices, incense and solemn assemblies, and will not listen to prayers from hands full of blood. It ends with the same list of deeds, 'Seek justice and correct the oppressor. Defend the fatherless and plead the case of the widow.' Isaiah 58 returns to the theme with fasting as the test case.

Asked about the fasts kept for seventy years, God replies, 'was it really for Me that you fasted?' and says to administer true justice and not oppress the widow, the fatherless, the foreigner or the poor. It is the closest parallel to Isaiah 58, and shows that the people's fasts had missed the point.

The Day of Atonement is the one fast the law required, with the instruction that the people humble themselves. Isaiah 58:3 and 5 use the same idiom. The prophet is speaking about the most sacred form of self-denial in the calendar, which makes the charge more serious.

God says He hates the feasts and will not hear the music of harps, and calls instead for justice to roll like a river and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream. Amos and Isaiah 58 share the idea that religious activity that ignores the oppressed is an offense to God and not a gift.

Zedekiah and the people freed their slaves and then took them back, and God said they had not proclaimed freedom. It shows the yokes of Isaiah 58:6 as actual practices in Jerusalem and explains why God treats the failure to release as a breach of the covenant.

The Sabbath commandment gives rest to servants and foreigners and ends with the reminder that Israel was a slave in Egypt. It binds the Sabbath to the freeing of the oppressed, which is why Isaiah can move from the yoke in verse 6 to the Sabbath in verse 13 without a break in thought.

Jesus reads the scroll of Isaiah in the synagogue on the Sabbath, includes the words 'to release the oppressed,' which echo Isaiah 58:6, and announces that the Scripture is fulfilled that day. It places the work of Isaiah 58 at the start of His public ministry.

On a Sabbath, Jesus frees a woman who had been bent over for eighteen years, and says she should be released from her bondage on that day. It is Isaiah 58:6 and 13 acted out together, loosing a yoke on a holy day as a delight and not a violation.

The King says that when the hungry were fed, the stranger welcomed and the naked clothed, it was done for Him. It carries the list of Isaiah 58:7 into the judgment and makes the acts of true fasting a matter of how we treat Christ in the least of His people.

Jesus tells His disciples not to disfigure their faces when they fast, but to anoint their heads and wash their faces so that the fast is known only to the Father. It treats the show of verse 5 as a hypocrisy and keeps fasting while turning it toward God.

Faith without deeds is dead, and wishing a hungry brother well without feeding him is worthless. James brings the argument of Isaiah 58:7 into the life of the church, and shows that the demand for deeds is not a contradiction of faith but its test.

A Sabbath rest remains for the people of God, and whoever enters it rests from his own work as God did. It shows what the Sabbath of Isaiah 58:13-14 points toward, a rest in which delight in the LORD is complete.

study.oneStory:
The Sabbath is older than Israel. God rested on the seventh day and blessed it, Genesis 2:2-3, and the Sabbath belongs to the world as it was meant to be. When God brought Israel out of Egypt, He joined that rest to freedom, since the people who had no rest under Pharaoh were to give rest to their servants and the foreigner among them, Deuteronomy 5:14-15. The yoke that God broke at the exodus was never meant to be put on a neighbor. The year of Jubilee extended the logic, with liberty proclaimed throughout the land, Leviticus 25:10.

The history of Israel is a long account of failing to live by it. Jeremiah's generation freed their slaves and took them back, and the prophet said God would proclaim freedom for them, freedom to fall by the sword, Jeremiah 34:17. The exile is, in part, God's answer to a people who kept the forms of worship and kept their neighbors in chains. Isaiah 58 comes in the midst of that story, speaking to a people who have begun to return and who are tempted to repeat it.

Isaiah's answer is also a promise. If the people would break the yoke, light would rise and ruins would be rebuilt, and they would be a garden that does not fail. That hope is not simply deferred. It is taken up in Isaiah 61, where a figure anointed by the Spirit comes to proclaim liberty, and in Luke 4, where Jesus says that He is that figure. In Him the Sabbath finds its Lord, the oppressed find their liberator, and the hungry find the One who says He was hungry too.

The early church lived this out. Believers sold property and shared with anyone in need, so that there were no needy ones among them, Acts 2:44-45 and 4:34-35. The apostles' letters keep calling for the same thing, and the church that cares for orphans and widows is doing what the chosen fast describes. The fast of the church is not the fast of the people in Isaiah 58, because they know their sins are paid for and that their deeds are the response of grateful people, not an attempt to be heard.

The end of the story fulfills the promises of verses 8 to 12. In the new creation the redeemed 'will never again hunger and never thirst,' and the Lamb will lead them to springs of living water, Revelation 7:16-17. The well-watered garden becomes a city with a river and a tree, Revelation 22:1-2, the age-old foundations are laid for good, and the Sabbath rest that remains for the people of God, Hebrews 4:9, becomes the unbroken delight of those who dwell in the presence of the LORD.

quiz.q: Why does God say Israel's fasting in verses 3-5 goes unnoticed?

options.text: Because it is paired with oppressing workers, quarreling, and striking with a wicked fist rather than justice.
options.note: Verses 3-4 name the specific injustice accompanying their fast.

options.text: Because they did not fast for enough days.
options.note: The problem is the injustice accompanying the fast, not its duration.

options.text: Because fasting itself is forbidden by God.
options.note: The chapter sharply critiques their fasting, but it redefines rather than forbids fasting outright.

options.text: Because they fasted in the wrong season of the year.
options.note: Timing is not the issue named in the text; injustice is.

quiz.q: According to verses 6-7, what does the fast God has chosen look like?

options.text: Breaking chains of wickedness, sharing bread with the hungry, and bringing the homeless into your home.
options.note: These verses give a concrete, active description of true fasting as justice and mercy.

options.text: Longer periods of self-denial and stricter sackcloth and ashes.
options.note: This is exactly the old form the chapter questions in verse 5, asking whether that alone constitutes an acceptable fast.

options.text: Avoiding all food and water for extended periods with no other requirement.
options.note: The chosen fast is defined by justice and mercy, not extended abstinence alone.

options.text: Withdrawing from society to focus solely on private prayer.
options.note: The chosen fast is explicitly about active engagement with the needs of others.

quiz.q: What promise is given to those who honor the Sabbath as a delight, verses 13-14?

options.text: They will delight in the LORD, ride on the heights of the land, and be fed with Jacob's heritage.
They will be exempt from all future hardship.
options.note: The promise is real blessing, but it is specific, delight and inheritance, not a blanket exemption from all hardship.

options.text: They will receive no reward, since Sabbath-keeping is purely symbolic.
options.note: The text gives a real, specific promise of blessing.

options.text: They will be forbidden from any rest on other days.
options.note: The passage promotes Sabbath delight, not a prohibition on rest at other times.

quiz.q: How does Jesus' mission statement in Luke 4:18 relate to this chapter?

options.text: It echoes Isaiah's language of freeing the oppressed and breaking every yoke, applying it to His own ministry.
options.note: Jesus draws His mission language from this section of Isaiah's prophecy of liberty for the oppressed.

options.text: It has no connection to this passage.
options.note: The connection in language and theme is direct.

options.text: It reverses Isaiah's meaning to focus only on personal piety.
options.note: Jesus' mission emphasizes active liberation and good news to the poor, matching Isaiah's emphasis.

options.text: It applies only to physical prisoners, not any other kind of oppression.
options.note: Literal captives are included, but the mission statement, like Isaiah's fast, addresses broader oppression, not solely literal imprisonment.

questions: Israel fasted while oppressing their workers and quarreling. Where might your own religious practice, church attendance, prayer, giving, be disconnected from how you actually treat people?

The fast God chose was breaking chains, feeding the hungry, and welcoming the homeless. What is one concrete act of justice or mercy you could do this week rather than simply another private discipline?
Verse 7 says not to turn away from your own flesh and blood. Is there a family member or close relationship you have been neglecting while attending to more distant, easier acts of charity?
God promises light, healing, and guidance to those who live this way. Where do you need that promised light and healing in your own life right now?
The Sabbath is described as a delight, not a burden. Is rest, in whatever form God calls you to it, something you actually delight in, or something you resent or ignore?

translationNotes.note: Cry aloud like a ram's horn renders shophar language elsewhere used for alarm or summons; the prophet is commanded to sound this indictment as urgently as a trumpet call to battle.

Repairer of the Breach and Restorer of the Streets of Dwelling are honorific titles, likely referring to literal rebuilding of Jerusalem's ruined walls and streets as well as the restoration of broken community life.
